title: Neuroimaging I: CT
summary: Reading head CT: densities, emergencies and a systematic approach.

lessons.title: How CT Works

levels.kid:
A CT scanner is a big donut-shaped camera. You lie on a bed, and the bed slides into the hole. Inside, an X-ray light spins around your head really fast and takes pictures from every side.

A computer puts all those pictures together, like stacking slices of bread to make a whole loaf. Then doctors can look at your brain one slice at a time.

Things that stop X-rays, like bone, look white. Air looks black. The brain looks gray. Fresh blood looks brighter than brain, so doctors can spot a bleed fast. The whole scan takes less than a minute!
levels.hs:
Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays, but instead of one flat picture it takes measurements from hundreds of angles as an X-ray tube spins around the patient. A computer then rebuilds those measurements into cross-sectional slices, like looking at the brain as a stack of thin slices.

Each tiny square (pixel) in a slice gets a number called a Hounsfield unit (HU), which tells you how much that spot blocks X-rays compared with water. Water is set at 0. Air is about -1000 and looks black. Fat is a little below zero and looks dark gray. Brain is around +20 to +40. Fresh blood is denser than brain, roughly +50 to +80, so it looks brighter. Bone is several hundred to over +1000 and looks white.

Doctors use words like hyperdense (brighter than brain), hypodense (darker) and isodense (the same). Because CT is fast, available in almost every emergency department, and excellent at showing blood and bone, it is usually the first scan for head injury and suspected stroke. Its downsides are radiation exposure and being less sensitive than MRI for small or very early strokes and for the back of the brain.
levels.college:
CT measures X-ray attenuation. A rotating tube and an opposing detector array record transmitted intensity from many projections; reconstruction algorithms (classically filtered back projection, now usually iterative or deep-learning reconstruction) compute the linear attenuation coefficient of each voxel. That value is rescaled to the Hounsfield scale: HU = 1000 × (μ tissue − μ water) / (μ water − μ air). By definition water is 0 and air is -1000.

Typical head values: CSF about 0 to +15, white matter about +25, gray matter about +35 to +40 (gray is slightly denser than white, which is why the cortex and deep nuclei look a touch brighter), acute clotted blood about +50 to +80, calcification above about +100, dense cortical bone up to and beyond +1000.

The eye can only separate a few dozen gray shades, so we use windowing. The window level sets the center HU and the window width sets the range mapped from black to white. A brain window (narrow, centered near +40) separates gray from white matter; a subdural or blood window (wider) helps see thin collections next to bright bone; a bone window (very wide, high center) shows fractures.

Artifacts matter. Beam hardening creates dark streaks between dense structures, classically between the petrous temporal bones across the pons. Partial volume averaging blurs small structures that occupy part of a voxel. Motion causes streaking and blur. Metal (clips, coils, fillings) causes star-shaped streaks.

Strengths: speed, availability, compatibility with monitors and most implants, superb for acute hemorrhage, fractures and hydrocephalus. Limits: ionizing radiation, poor sensitivity for hyperacute ischemia and posterior fossa pathology compared with MRI.
levels.phd:
The physics of CT is the physics of the linear attenuation coefficient μ, which depends on electron density, effective atomic number and photon energy. At diagnostic energies, Compton scattering (dependent on electron density) and the photoelectric effect (strongly dependent on atomic number, roughly Z cubed, and falling steeply with energy) dominate. Because the tube emits a polychromatic spectrum, lower-energy photons are preferentially absorbed as the beam passes dense material, so the beam's mean energy rises along its path. This beam hardening violates the monoenergetic assumption of reconstruction and produces cupping and dark streak artifacts, which is why the posterior fossa is the weakest region of a head CT.

Reconstruction is an inverse problem. Filtered back projection is an analytic solution derived from the Radon transform and Fourier slice theorem; it is fast but noisy at low dose. Iterative reconstruction models photon statistics and system geometry, allowing substantial dose reduction at equal image quality, and newer deep-learning reconstruction learns noise texture directly.

Dual-energy CT acquires attenuation at two spectra, which lets the scanner decompose voxels into basis materials. Clinically this separates iodine from blood after thrombectomy (contrast staining versus true hemorrhage), creates virtual non-contrast images, and identifies calcium. Photon-counting detectors go further, counting individual photons and binning them by energy, which improves spatial resolution and reduces electronic noise.

Hounsfield values of blood are not fixed: attenuation reflects hemoglobin and protein concentration. Clot retraction concentrates hemoglobin, which is why acute clot is denser than flowing blood. A severely anemic patient's acute hematoma can look nearly isodense, and coagulopathic or hyperacute bleeding can look heterogeneous. Understanding these determinants turns gray-scale reading from pattern recognition into reasoning about tissue composition.
levels.expert:
In practice, CT is the gatekeeper scan for almost every acute neurosurgical problem, and knowing its blind spots is as important as knowing what it shows.

How a senior reader thinks:
- Always scroll in at least three windows: brain, subdural (blood) and bone. Thin subdurals hide against the inner table in a narrow brain window, and nondisplaced fractures are invisible without the bone window.
- Use multiplanar reformats. Coronal images reveal subdurals along the tentorium and falx and help judge skull base fractures; sagittal images help with the posterior fossa and the craniocervical junction.
- Remember density is relative and patient-dependent. Anemia makes blood less dense; a very high hematocrit makes normal dural sinuses look bright and can mimic thrombosis or a hyperdense artery.
- Respect artifacts. Beam hardening across the pons can mimic or hide a brainstem lesion; the answer is MRI, not over-calling.
- After thrombectomy, a bright area may be contrast staining rather than blood. Dual-energy CT or a follow-up scan in about a day clarifies it, and this distinction changes whether antithrombotics can start.

Radiation and stewardship: a head CT carries an effective dose of roughly a couple of millisieverts, small but not zero, and children are more radiosensitive. Validated decision rules (for example the Canadian CT Head Rule and PECARN in children) exist so that we scan the patients who need it, not everyone who bumps their head.

When CT is the wrong tool: suspected early posterior circulation stroke, small infarcts, encephalitis, demyelination, and most tumors characterize far better on MRI. CT gets you the life-saving answer in minutes — is there blood, mass effect or hydrocephalus — and MRI usually explains the rest.

keyPoints: CT rebuilds X-ray attenuation from many angles into cross-sectional slices.
Hounsfield units: water 0, air -1000, brain about +20 to +40, acute blood about +50 to +80, bone up to +1000 or more.
Hyperdense = brighter than brain; hypodense = darker.
Windowing (level and width) chooses which HU range is displayed; read brain, subdural and bone windows.
Beam hardening creates streaks in the posterior fossa; MRI is better there.
CT is fast and ideal for blood, bone and hydrocephalus but less sensitive than MRI for early ischemia.

test.q: What does a Hounsfield unit measure?
test.explain: HU rescale each voxel's X-ray attenuation so water is 0 and air is -1000.

test.q: Which has the highest Hounsfield value?
test.explain: Dense cortical bone is several hundred to over +1000 HU; acute blood is about +50 to +80.

test.q: By definition, water has a Hounsfield value of ___.
test.explain: The scale is anchored at water = 0 and air = -1000.

test.q: What one-word term describes a region brighter than normal brain on CT?
test.explain: Hyperdense (hyperattenuating) means it blocks more X-rays than brain, like acute blood.

test.q: Why does gray matter look slightly brighter than white matter on CT?
choices: It has slightly higher density (less myelin lipid)
It has more myelin lipid, which raises attenuation
It has more water, which is denser than tissue
It lies near the skull and gets beam-hardening glow
test.explain: White matter's myelin is lipid-rich, lowering its attenuation, so gray matter is a little denser.

test.q: Which window best shows a skull fracture?
test.explain: A very wide, high-level bone window displays cortical detail and fracture lines.

test.q: Dark streaks between dense bones caused by preferential absorption of low-energy photons are called beam ___.
test.explain: Beam hardening is classic across the pons between the petrous temporal bones.

test.q: Which is a major limitation of CT compared with MRI?
choices: It shows acute blood less clearly than MRI does
It is less sensitive for very early ischemic stroke
It takes much longer than MRI to acquire images
It shows bone poorly compared with MRI sequences
test.explain: CT is often normal in the first hours of ischemia; MRI diffusion imaging detects it within minutes.

test.q: What is the Hounsfield value of air?
test.explain: Air is defined as -1000 HU and appears black.

test.q: Why is acute clotted blood denser than flowing blood?
choices: Clot retraction concentrates hemoglobin and protein
Clot takes up calcium deposits within minutes
Clot traps tiny gas bubbles that raise density
Clot cools below body temperature and condenses
test.explain: Retraction squeezes out serum, concentrating hemoglobin, raising attenuation.

test.q: Why is CT usually the first scan in head trauma?
choices: It uses no ionizing radiation, which suits young trauma patients
It is fast, widely available and excellent for blood and bone
It best shows diffuse axonal injury and white matter tracts
It needs IV contrast, which highlights active bleeding
test.explain: Speed and sensitivity to hemorrhage and fractures make CT the trauma workhorse.

kidTest.q: What shape is a CT scanner?
kidTest.explain: You slide through a donut-shaped ring.

kidTest.q: What color is bone on CT?
kidTest.explain: Bone stops X-rays, so it looks white.

kidTest.q: What color is air on CT?
kidTest.explain: Air lets X-rays through, so it looks black.

kidTest.q: Fresh blood looks ___ than brain.
kidTest.explain: Fresh blood is denser, so it looks brighter.

kidTest.q: CT scans use what kind of rays?
kidTest.explain: CT uses X-rays from many angles.

kidTest.q: How long does a head CT take?
kidTest.explain: The scan itself is very fast.

advancedTest.q: After thrombectomy a hyperdense area appears in the basal ganglia. What best distinguishes iodine staining from hemorrhage?
advancedTest.explain: Dual-energy CT separates iodine from blood; a follow-up scan also shows staining washing out.

advancedTest.q: Why is the photoelectric effect especially important for contrast and calcium?
choices: It depends strongly on atomic number
It does not depend on photon energy
advancedTest.explain: Photoelectric absorption rises steeply with atomic number, so iodine and calcium attenuate strongly.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a very high hematocrit has bright dural sinuses on noncontrast CT. What is the main pitfall?
choices: Mistaking it for venous sinus thrombosis
Missing a skull base fracture near the sinus
advancedTest.explain: High hematocrit raises blood density, mimicking the dense sinus of thrombosis; measure HU and correlate with venography.

lessons.title: A Systematic Head CT Read

levels.kid:
When doctors look at a brain scan, they follow the same checklist every time, like a pilot before takeoff. That way they don't miss anything.

A fun way to remember it is "Blood Can Be Very Bad." Blood: is there any bleeding? Cisterns: are the little pools of brain water around the brainstem open? Brain: does the brain look normal on both sides? Ventricles: are the water rooms in the middle the right size? Bone: is the skull cracked?

Checking in the same order every time is how good doctors catch tiny problems.
levels.hs:
Radiologists and neurosurgeons read head CTs with a fixed checklist so that an obvious finding doesn't distract them from a second, subtler one. A popular mnemonic is "Blood Can Be Very Bad":

- Blood: look for bright (hyperdense) blood anywhere: over the brain surface, inside the brain, in the ventricles, or in the spaces around the brain.
- Cisterns: the basal cisterns are CSF spaces around the brainstem. If they are squeezed shut (effaced), pressure inside the skull is dangerously high.
- Brain: compare left and right. Is the gray-white boundary sharp? Is there a dark area (stroke or swelling) or a mass? Is the midline shifted?
- Ventricles: are they too big (hydrocephalus), squeezed, or pushed to one side?
- Bone: switch to the bone window and look for fractures, plus air where it shouldn't be.

After that, check the soft tissues of the scalp (a swelling marks where the head was hit), the sinuses and the mastoid air cells. Fluid in the sinuses after trauma can hint at a skull base fracture.

Finally, compare with any earlier scan. A small bleed that is growing is much more worrying than one that is stable.
levels.college:
A systematic read prevents satisfaction of search, the error of stopping after the first abnormality. Work through "Blood Can Be Very Bad" plus extras:

Blood: search every compartment — epidural, subdural (including along the falx and tentorium), subarachnoid (sylvian fissures, interpeduncular cistern, sulci), intraparenchymal and intraventricular (dependent occipital horns are a favorite hiding place).

Cisterns: identify the suprasellar cistern (star or pentagon shape), ambient cisterns around the midbrain, and the quadrigeminal cistern. Effacement indicates mass effect and impending transtentorial herniation; blood in them suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Brain: assess gray-white differentiation (loss suggests infarction or diffuse hypoxic injury), symmetry, hypodensities, masses, and midline shift. Measure shift as the perpendicular distance from the septum pellucidum to a line joining the anterior and posterior falx attachments.

Ventricles: size and shape. Enlarged temporal horns are an early sign of hydrocephalus. Distinguish communicating from obstructive patterns: a dilated lateral and third ventricle with a small fourth suggests aqueductal obstruction. Look for trapped or compressed ventricles.

Bone: on bone windows, check the calvarium, skull base, orbits, and facial bones. Pneumocephalus (air) implies a breach of the dura or sinus. Opacified mastoids or sphenoid sinus after trauma raise suspicion for a skull base fracture.

Extras: scalp hematoma (coup site), foreign bodies, lines and devices (shunt catheter position, external ventricular drain tip), the orbits, and the top of the cervical spine. Always compare with priors and correlate with the clinical question.
levels.phd:
A systematic search strategy addresses a well-documented cognitive problem in diagnostic imaging. Eye-tracking studies show that experts make an early global impression and then direct focused scanning, while novices search inefficiently; both groups are vulnerable to satisfaction of search, where detecting one lesion lowers the probability of detecting a second. Structured checklists measurably reduce these misses, especially for findings with low prior probability.

The anatomy behind the checklist is pressure physiology. The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that, within a rigid skull, brain, blood and CSF volumes must sum to a constant; an expanding mass is initially buffered by displacing CSF and venous blood. On CT this buffer is visible: sulci flatten, ventricles compress and the basal cisterns narrow. Once the buffer is exhausted, small volume increases produce steep rises in intracranial pressure along an exponential pressure-volume curve. Cisternal effacement on CT is therefore a structural marker that the patient is on the steep part of that curve.

Midline shift quantifies lateral displacement; in traumatic injury, greater shift at the septum pellucidum correlates with worse outcome and is a component of prognostic models such as the Rotterdam CT score, which also includes basal cistern status, traumatic subarachnoid or intraventricular blood, and the presence of an epidural mass lesion.

Gray-white differentiation reflects the small density difference between cortex and myelinated white matter. Diffuse loss of that contrast after cardiac arrest, sometimes with a 'pseudo-subarachnoid' appearance as swollen brain makes normal vessels look relatively bright, signals severe global hypoxic-ischemic injury.

Finally, the read is Bayesian: the clinical question sets the prior. The same subtle hypodensity carries different meaning in a patient with sudden aphasia than in an asymptomatic scan, which is why the history belongs in every request.
levels.expert:
On call, a neurosurgeon reads the CT before the formal report arrives, so the system has to be fast, complete and tied to decisions.

My order on a trauma or deterioration scan:
- Scout image first: fractures, foreign bodies, cervical alignment, and whether the whole head was covered.
- Blood in every compartment, in brain and subdural windows. Then ask: is it surgical? Thickness, volume, midline shift and the patient's exam drive that call.
- Cisterns: open, compressed or absent. Absent cisterns with a dilated contralateral temporal horn (from compression of CSF outflow) is a scan that means the operating room or urgent pressure management now.
- Ventricles: hydrocephalus may need an external ventricular drain, especially in posterior fossa hemorrhage or intraventricular blood.
- Bone and air: depressed fractures, skull base involvement, pneumocephalus.
- Devices and lines: shunt and drain positions.
- Priors: compare measurements, not impressions.

Pitfalls I see in trainees:
- Missing a thin isodense subdural in an older patient because both hemispheres are symmetrically compressed. Look for sulci that don't reach the inner table and inward-displaced cortical veins.
- Calling falx calcification or a dense falx a subdural; check bone window density.
- Forgetting the posterior fossa and the foramen magnum, where tonsillar crowding and cerebellar hematomas hide.
- Treating a 'negative' early CT as ruling out stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Timing matters.

Communicate findings with what matters for action: compartment, size, shift, cisternal status, hydrocephalus and change from prior. "Right acute subdural, 12 millimeters, 8 millimeters of shift, cisterns effaced" tells the team everything they need in one sentence.

keyPoints: Use a fixed checklist to avoid satisfaction of search: Blood, Cisterns, Brain, Ventricles, Bone.
Effaced basal cisterns signal high intracranial pressure and herniation risk.
Midline shift is measured at the septum pellucidum.
Enlarged temporal horns are an early sign of hydrocephalus.
Check bone windows, sinuses, mastoids, scalp, devices and compare with priors.

examples.tr: Intraventricular hemorrhage layering in dependent ventricles; easy to miss.

test.q: In 'Blood Can Be Very Bad', what does the C stand for?
test.explain: C = cisterns, the CSF spaces around the brainstem.

test.q: What is 'satisfaction of search'?
choices: Reading too slowly after the first abnormal finding
Missing a second finding after spotting the first
Using the wrong window and missing subtle blood
Ordering more scans until one shows a finding
test.explain: Finding one abnormality lowers detection of others; a checklist counters it.

test.q: Midline shift is usually measured at the septum ___.
test.explain: The septum pellucidum is the midline membrane between the lateral ventricles.

test.q: Effaced basal cisterns most strongly suggest:
test.explain: Mass effect squeezes the cisterns, a warning of herniation.

test.q: Which part of the lateral ventricles enlarges early in hydrocephalus? (two words)
test.explain: Dilated temporal horns are an early, sensitive sign.

test.q: A dilated lateral and third ventricle with a small fourth ventricle suggests obstruction at the:
test.explain: Blockage at the aqueduct dilates everything upstream but not the fourth ventricle.

test.q: Fluid in the sphenoid sinus after head trauma raises concern for:
test.explain: Blood in the sinus can mark a basal skull fracture.

test.q: Air inside the skull is called ___.
test.explain: Pneumocephalus implies a breach of dura or a sinus, or recent surgery.

test.q: What does the Monro-Kellie doctrine state?
choices: Brain, blood and CSF volumes in the skull sum to a constant
CSF is made in the spinal cord and absorbed in the skull
Intracranial pressure rises linearly with each added volume
The skull expands slightly to absorb a rise in volume
test.explain: In a rigid skull, an increase in one component must be offset by others.

test.q: In the mnemonic, the final 'B' stands for which tissue checked on its own window?
test.explain: Bone window review finds fractures.

test.q: Why compare with prior scans?
choices: Prior scans are usually normal anyway
test.explain: An enlarging hematoma or new hydrocephalus may need urgent action.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors use a checklist to read scans?
kidTest.explain: Same order every time means fewer misses.

kidTest.q: 'Blood Can Be Very Bad' starts with checking for…
kidTest.explain: First look for bleeding.

kidTest.q: Ventricles are…
choices: Teeth hiding in the back of your mouth
Water rooms in the middle of the brain
Hair growing on the top of your head
kidTest.explain: They hold brain fluid.

kidTest.q: What does the last B stand for? (the hard part of your head)
kidTest.explain: Bone: check the skull for cracks.

kidTest.q: Doctors compare the left and right sides of the brain because…
kidTest.explain: Differences can show a problem.

advancedTest.q: Diffuse loss of gray-white differentiation with bright-appearing basal cisterns after cardiac arrest most likely represents:
choices: True subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm
Pseudo-subarachnoid sign from global hypoxic-ischemic edema
advancedTest.explain: Swollen hypodense brain makes normal vessels and dura look relatively dense.

advancedTest.q: Which feature is part of the Rotterdam CT score?
advancedTest.explain: Rotterdam includes basal cisterns, midline shift, epidural mass and traumatic SAH/IVH.

advancedTest.q: Bilateral isodense subdurals can be missed because:
choices: They are hyperdense and blend into the bright skull
They show up on bone window rather than brain window
They occur mainly in infants with open fontanelles
Symmetric compression removes the midline shift clue
advancedTest.explain: Look for sulci not reaching the inner table and displaced cortical veins.

lessons.title: Hemorrhage on CT

levels.kid:
Sometimes a blood vessel in or around the brain breaks and leaks. On a CT scan, fresh blood looks bright white-gray, brighter than brain.

Where the blood sits gives it a name. Blood shaped like a lemon pressed against the skull is an epidural bleed. Blood shaped like a banana spreading along the skull is a subdural bleed. Blood in the little cracks and pools around the brain is a subarachnoid bleed. And blood inside the brain itself is an intracerebral bleed.

Knowing the shape helps doctors decide if surgery is needed right away.
levels.hs:
Acute blood is hyperdense on CT, and its shape tells you which space it's in.

- Epidural hematoma (EDH): between the skull and the dura. It looks like a lens (biconvex), because the dura is stuck tightly at the skull sutures, so the blood can't spread past them. It often comes from a torn middle meningeal artery after a skull fracture over the temple. Classic story: a brief knockout, a 'lucid interval' where the person seems fine, then rapid decline.
- Subdural hematoma (SDH): between the dura and the brain. It looks like a crescent that can cross suture lines but not the midline. It comes from torn bridging veins and is common in older adults and people on blood thinners.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH): blood in the CSF spaces around the brain, filling sulci and cisterns. Without trauma, the most common cause is a ruptured aneurysm, often felt as the 'worst headache of my life.'
- Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH): bleeding inside brain tissue, often from high blood pressure in deep areas like the basal ganglia.
- Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH): blood in the ventricles.

Blood changes with time. A subdural is bright when fresh, becomes the same gray as brain after about one to three weeks, then turns dark as it becomes chronic.
levels.college:
Compartment determines mechanism, urgency and treatment.

Epidural hematoma: biconvex, sharply marginated, limited by sutures (where the periosteal dura adheres) but able to cross the midline and tentorium because it lies outside the dural reflections. Usually arterial (middle meningeal artery, temporal squamous fracture); venous EDHs occur near dural sinuses. A 'swirl sign' — hypodense areas within a hyperdense collection — indicates unclotted, actively bleeding blood.

Subdural hematoma: crescentic, crosses sutures, stopped by dural reflections (falx, tentorium) so it does not cross the midline, though it can track along the falx and tentorium. Bridging vein tears from acceleration-deceleration; atrophy (aging, alcohol-related brain atrophy) and anticoagulation increase risk. Density evolves: acute hyperdense, subacute isodense (roughly 1–3 weeks), chronic hypodense. Mixed density suggests acute-on-chronic bleeding.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage: hyperdensity in sulci, sylvian fissures, interhemispheric fissure and basal cisterns. Aneurysmal SAH centers on the basal cisterns; perimesencephalic SAH (blood anterior to the midbrain and pons) has a benign course; convexity SAH suggests reversible cerebral vasoconstriction or amyloid angiopathy. Modern CT is extremely sensitive within about six hours of headache onset; sensitivity declines afterward, which is why a lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia is used when CT is negative later.

Intracerebral hemorrhage: hypertensive bleeds favor the putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum; lobar bleeds in older adults suggest cerebral amyloid angiopathy; atypical locations or young patients prompt a search for vascular malformations, tumors or venous thrombosis. Volume can be estimated as ABC/2.

Intraventricular hemorrhage may be primary or extend from ICH or SAH and risks obstructive hydrocephalus.
levels.phd:
Hemorrhage density is a function of hemoglobin concentration, protein content and clot structure. Immediately after extravasation, liquid blood measures roughly +40 to +60 HU; clot formation and retraction raise this toward +60 to +80 HU or more over hours. As red cells lyse and protein is broken down and resorbed, attenuation falls by around one to two HU per day, producing the isodense subacute phase and the hypodense chronic phase. This explains several traps: hyperacute bleeding, coagulopathic blood that fails to retract, and severe anemia can all yield lower-than-expected densities, and the 'swirl sign' reflects mixed liquid and clotted components that signal ongoing extravasation.

The geometry of extra-axial collections follows dural anatomy. The periosteal layer of dura adheres to the inner table most firmly at sutures, so arterial epidural blood under pressure strips dura locally and bulges inward into a lens. Subdural blood occupies a potential space created by cleavage within the dural border cell layer, so it spreads freely along the convexity until a dural reflection stops it.

Chronic subdural hematoma is not simply old blood. It is an inflammatory, angiogenic process: neomembranes with fragile, leaky capillaries, local fibrinolysis and repeated microbleeding sustain and enlarge the collection. This biology underlies recurrence after drainage and motivates middle meningeal artery embolization, which devascularizes the membranes; randomized trials published in 2024 showed lower recurrence when embolization was added to standard care.

In intracerebral hemorrhage, hematoma expansion occurs in a substantial minority of patients, mostly within the first hours, and strongly predicts death and disability. Imaging markers of expansion include the CTA spot sign (contrast extravasation within the clot) and noncontrast signs such as heterogeneous density, the blend sign, the black hole sign and irregular shape. These markers shaped trials of hemostatic and blood pressure interventions, which aim to stop growth during that early window.
levels.expert:
Hemorrhage on CT becomes a surgical decision through a few numbers, the exam and the trajectory.

Traumatic thresholds used in Brain Trauma Foundation guidance (the published surgical management guidelines): an acute epidural over about 30 milliliters generally warrants evacuation regardless of GCS; an acute subdural thicker than about 10 millimeters or with midline shift over about 5 millimeters generally warrants evacuation regardless of GCS. Smaller lesions in an awake patient may be observed with serial imaging and neuro checks, but a temporal epidural near the uncus deserves a low threshold because the room to decompensate is small.

Practical points:
- The swirl sign and a hematoma that has grown on a repeat scan change 'watch' to 'go.'
- Reverse anticoagulation fast in any intracranial bleed. Know the reversal agents for each anticoagulant class and involve hematology or pharmacy.
- In nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage, get a CTA immediately to look for an aneurysm, and watch for hydrocephalus, which may need an external ventricular drain before anything else.
- Cerebellar hemorrhage with brainstem compression, hydrocephalus or neurological decline is a classic indication for suboccipital decompression; posterior fossa space is unforgiving.
- Supratentorial ICH surgery is selective; minimally invasive evacuation of lobar hematomas showed benefit in the 2024 ENRICH trial, and decisions depend on location, size, depth and deficits.
- Lobar ICH in an older adult: think amyloid angiopathy and plan MRI with susceptibility imaging. In a young patient: think malformation and get vascular imaging.
- Chronic subdural in an older patient: burr hole drainage for symptoms, consider middle meningeal artery embolization to lower recurrence.

Report the compartment, size, shift, cisterns, hydrocephalus and expansion signs. Those six facts drive almost every call.

keyPoints: Epidural: biconvex, limited by sutures, usually middle meningeal artery; lucid interval.
Subdural: crescent, crosses sutures but not the midline; bridging veins; elderly and anticoagulated.
SDH density: acute bright, subacute isodense (about 1–3 weeks), chronic dark.
SAH: blood in sulci and cisterns; nontraumatic cause most often a ruptured aneurysm.
Hypertensive ICH: putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum; lobar ICH in elderly suggests amyloid angiopathy.
Swirl sign and CTA spot sign predict active bleeding and expansion.

test.q: Which hematoma is lens-shaped and limited by sutures?
test.explain: Dura adheres at sutures, so epidural blood bulges into a biconvex lens.

test.q: A subdural hematoma usually comes from:
test.explain: Torn bridging veins between cortex and dural sinuses bleed into the subdural space.

test.q: Which collection can cross sutures but not the midline?
test.explain: Subdurals spread along the convexity but are stopped by the falx.

test.q: A brief knockout followed by a period of seeming normal, then decline, is called a lucid ___.
test.explain: Classic, though not universal, in epidural hematoma.

test.q: A subdural that is the same density as brain is most likely:
test.explain: Around one to three weeks the subdural becomes isodense.

test.q: What is the most common cause of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage?

lessons.title: Infarct, Edema & Mass Effect

levels.kid:
A stroke happens when a blood vessel gets blocked and part of the brain doesn't get enough blood. In the first few hours, a CT scan might look almost normal! Later, the hurt part turns darker gray.

Sometimes hurt brain swells, like a sprained ankle puffs up. But the skull is hard like a helmet and can't stretch. So the swelling pushes the brain sideways or down. Doctors call this mass effect.

If the pushing gets really bad, surgeons can take off a piece of skull to give the brain room, then put it back later when the swelling goes down.
levels.hs:
An ischemic stroke (infarct) is brain tissue dying from lack of blood flow. On CT it shows up as a dark (hypodense) area that matches the territory of a blood vessel. But in the first few hours the CT is often normal or shows only subtle signs:

- A hyperdense artery: a clot inside the middle cerebral artery can look bright, the 'hyperdense MCA sign.'
- Loss of the gray-white boundary: swollen gray matter loses its slightly brighter look.
- Loss of the insular ribbon and blurring of the lentiform nucleus deep in the brain.
- Sulcal effacement: the grooves on the brain surface flatten.

Edema means swelling. Cytotoxic edema happens when cells themselves swell, as in stroke; it affects both gray and white matter. Vasogenic edema is fluid leaking out of damaged blood vessels, as around tumors or abscesses; it spreads through white matter in finger-like shapes and spares the cortex.

Mass effect is what happens when swelling or a mass takes up space: sulci disappear, ventricles get squeezed, and the midline shifts. Push hard enough and brain tissue herniates, squeezing past rigid edges inside the skull. That can compress the brainstem and is life-threatening. A huge swollen stroke can be treated by removing part of the skull (decompressive craniectomy).
levels.college:
Early ischemic CT signs reflect cytotoxic edema: sodium-potassium pump failure draws water into cells, and each one percent increase in tissue water lowers attenuation by roughly 2.5 HU, so changes are subtle at first. Signs: hyperdense artery (MCA, basilar), insular ribbon sign, obscured lentiform nucleus, loss of gray-white differentiation and sulcal effacement. Frank hypodensity becomes clear over hours to a day.

ASPECTS (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score) quantifies early change in the MCA territory: start at 10 and subtract one for each of ten regions showing early ischemia (caudate, lentiform, internal capsule, insula, and six cortical regions M1–M6). Lower scores mean larger infarcts; scores of 6 or more traditionally favored thrombectomy, though recent trials support treatment in selected patients with larger cores.

Evolution: hypodensity and mass effect peak around days 3–5. At about 2–3 weeks the 'fogging' phenomenon can make an infarct transiently isodense. Chronic infarcts become CSF-density encephalomalacia with ex vacuo enlargement of adjacent ventricles. Hemorrhagic transformation may occur, especially after reperfusion.

Edema types: cytotoxic (intracellular, gray and white matter, vascular territory, restricted diffusion on MRI); vasogenic (extracellular, blood-brain barrier breakdown, white matter predominant, finger-like, around tumors, abscesses, contusions); interstitial (transependymal CSF in acute hydrocephalus, periventricular lucency).

Herniation types: subfalcine (cingulate under the falx; can compress the anterior cerebral artery), uncal transtentorial (medial temporal lobe over the tentorium; compresses CN III, causing a dilated pupil), central/descending, upward (from posterior fossa masses), tonsillar (through the foramen magnum, compressing the medulla), and external (through a skull defect).
levels.phd:
The CT density of an infarct is a readout of water physiology. Within minutes of critical flow reduction, ATP depletion halts Na+/K+-ATPase, sodium and water enter cells, and cytotoxic edema begins. This intracellular shift changes diffusion profoundly (detected by MRI) but changes total tissue water little, so CT barely moves. Over the following hours, ionic edema develops as sodium is drawn from blood across a still-intact barrier into the depleted extracellular space, net tissue water rises, and CT attenuation falls. Later, as the barrier breaks down, vasogenic edema and finally hemorrhagic transformation can follow. Net water uptake measured quantitatively on CT has been proposed as a tissue clock and as a predictor of malignant edema.

Malignant MCA infarction illustrates mass effect pathophysiology. A large territorial infarct in a young brain, without atrophy to buffer it, swells over two to five days; mortality with medical treatment alone was historically around 80 percent. Pooled analysis of the European trials (DECIMAL, DESTINY, HAMLET) showed that hemicraniectomy within 48 hours in patients up to 60 years old roughly halved mortality, and DESTINY II showed survival benefit in older patients, but at the cost of more survivors with severe disability, which makes this a values-based decision with families.

Herniation is not simply 'pressure.' Displacement compresses specific structures: uncal herniation stretches the oculomotor nerve against the tentorial edge and can compress the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the tentorium, causing hemiparesis ipsilateral to the lesion (Kernohan's notch, a false-localizing sign). Downward displacement stretches perforating branches of the basilar artery, producing midline brainstem 'Duret' hemorrhages. Subfalcine herniation can occlude the pericallosal artery, adding an anterior cerebral territory infarct on top of the original lesion.
levels.expert:
Two practical questions dominate: how much brain is already gone, and how much more will swell?

Early infarct on CT:
- Read for ASPECTS in a narrow window (some readers set a level near the gray-white midpoint and a narrow width to exaggerate contrast). Compare sides carefully and use thin slices.
- A hyperdense MCA or basilar sign with the right clinical picture means 'get the CTA now'; don't wait for the hypodensity.
- Remember mimics: old infarcts (sharply marginated, CSF-dense, with volume loss), low-grade tumors, encephalitis, and seizure-related changes.

Predicting dangerous swelling:
- Large MCA infarcts (more than half the territory), early hypodensity in over a third of the territory, involvement of additional territories, and younger age predict malignant edema.
- Discuss decompressive hemicraniectomy early, ideally before herniation, within the 48-hour window in which the trials showed benefit. The flap must be large, typically at least 12 centimeters in diameter, with a duraplasty, or it simply creates a mushroom of herniating brain.
- Cerebellar infarcts swell into the fourth ventricle and brainstem. Watch for drowsiness, new hydrocephalus and effacement of the fourth ventricle; suboccipital decompressive craniectomy, sometimes with an external ventricular drain, can be life-saving and outcomes in survivors are often good.

Distinguishing edema types guides therapy: vasogenic edema around tumors responds to corticosteroids; cytotoxic edema from stroke does not, and steroids are not used for ischemic stroke edema.

Herniation at the bedside: a unilateral dilated pupil, falling GCS, Cushing's response (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) — temporize with head elevation, osmotherapy, brief controlled hyperventilation as a bridge, and get the patient to definitive decompression.

keyPoints: Early infarct signs: hyperdense artery, insular ribbon loss, obscured lentiform nucleus, gray-white blurring, sulcal effacement.
ASPECTS scores 10 MCA regions; lower score = larger infarct.
Cytotoxic edema: cell swelling, gray and white matter, stroke. Vasogenic: leaky vessels, white matter, tumors; responds to steroids.
Infarct swelling peaks around days 3–5; fogging at 2–3 weeks.
Herniations: subfalcine, uncal, central, upward, tonsillar, external.
Malignant MCA infarction: hemicraniectomy within 48 hours reduces mortality.

lessons.title: CT Angiography & Perfusion

levels.kid:
Sometimes doctors need to see the blood pipes in the brain. They put a special dye into a vein in the arm. The dye travels to the brain and makes the blood vessels light up bright on the CT. This is called CT angiography.

It's like turning on lights in a dark tunnel. If a pipe is blocked by a clot, the light stops at that spot!

Another scan, called perfusion, watches how fast the dye flows into each part of the brain. It shows which parts are already hurt and which parts can still be saved if the pipe gets opened quickly.
levels.hs:
CT angiography (CTA) is a CT scan done while iodine contrast dye flows through the arteries. A fast scan timed to catch the dye in the arteries gives a 3D map of the blood vessels from the heart's arch up through the neck to the top of the head.

What CTA shows:
- A blocked large artery (large vessel occlusion) in a stroke, which can be removed by thrombectomy.
- Aneurysms (balloon-like bulges) after a subarachnoid hemorrhage.
- Narrowing of the carotid arteries, tears in artery walls (dissections), and abnormal tangles of vessels.
- A 'spot sign' of dye leaking into a brain bleed, meaning it may grow.

CT perfusion (CTP) scans the same slices again and again as the dye passes through. A computer measures blood flow, blood volume and how long blood takes to arrive in each area. This divides an ischemic stroke into two parts: the core, which is already dead, and the penumbra, which is starving but still alive. A small core with a big penumbra means there is a lot of brain worth saving, which helps doctors choose thrombectomy even many hours after a stroke began.

Contrast dye is generally safe. The main concerns are allergy-like reactions and kidney strain, but in an emergency stroke, doctors usually don't wait for kidney tests.
levels.college:
CTA uses a bolus of iodinated contrast with bolus tracking: the scanner monitors a region (for example the aortic arch) and triggers acquisition when enhancement crosses a threshold. Thin sections are reconstructed into maximum intensity projections (MIPs), multiplanar and 3D volume renderings.

Stroke uses: detect large vessel occlusion (ICA terminus, M1, proximal M2, basilar), assess the clot burden, tandem cervical lesions and access anatomy for thrombectomy, and grade collaterals. Multiphase CTA (arterial, peak venous, late venous phases) shows delayed collateral filling, a strong predictor of outcome.

Other uses: aneurysm detection (high sensitivity for aneurysms above roughly 3 millimeters; very small or skull-base-adjacent aneurysms may still need catheter angiography), dissection (tapering, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm), carotid stenosis, vascular malformations, and the ICH spot sign. CT venography visualizes the dural sinuses; the 'empty delta sign' (enhancing dural wall around a non-enhancing clot in the superior sagittal sinus) suggests venous sinus thrombosis.

CTP acquires repeated images during contrast transit and deconvolves tissue time-attenuation curves with an arterial input function to compute:
- CBF (cerebral blood flow), CBV (cerebral blood volume), MTT (mean transit time = CBV/CBF, from the central volume principle), and Tmax (time to the residue function maximum).
- Ischemic core is commonly estimated as relative CBF below 30 percent of normal tissue; hypoperfused tissue at risk as Tmax above 6 seconds. The difference is the penumbra.

Late-window selection: DEFUSE 3 (6–16 hours) used perfusion mismatch criteria; DAWN (6–24 hours) used a mismatch between clinical severity and core size. Both showed large benefits of thrombectomy.

Contrast-associated kidney injury risk is lower than once believed; in suspected large vessel occlusion, CTA should not be delayed for creatinine results.
levels.phd:
CT perfusion rests on indicator-dilution theory. Assuming a nondiffusible tracer and a linear relationship between iodine concentration and HU, the tissue concentration curve equals the arterial input function convolved with the tissue residue function scaled by CBF. Deconvolution (commonly by singular value decomposition, often a delay-insensitive block-circulant variant) recovers the flow-scaled residue function; its peak gives CBF, its area gives CBV, and their ratio gives MTT by the central volume theorem. Tmax, the time at which the residue function peaks, is highly sensitive to delayed arrival and dispersion of the bolus, which is why it flags hypoperfused tissue so well — and why it is also inflated by proximal stenosis or poor cardiac output, independent of true tissue risk.

Core estimation is an operational definition, not a histological one. Low CBF at a single moment predicts infarction if flow is not restored, but early, complete reperfusion can rescue tissue that met 'core' thresholds, producing the so-called ghost core: overestimation, most often when imaging occurs very early after onset. Conversely, core grows over time in patients who are slow progressors (good collaterals) or fast progressors (poor collaterals), and this individual variability is the biological reason why fixed time windows were replaced by tissue windows.

Autoregulation explains the perfusion patterns. In mild hypoperfusion, arteriolar dilation maintains CBF while CBV rises and MTT lengthens; as perfusion pressure falls further, autoregulation fails, CBF drops, and eventually CBV falls as the vascular bed collapses. Thus elevated MTT with preserved or high CBV implies salvageable tissue; matched low CBF and low CBV implies core.

Newer large-core trials (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, TENSION, TESLA and others in 2023–2024) showed that thrombectomy benefits even many patients with large estimated cores, loosening the role of perfusion as a strict gatekeeper. Perfusion remains valuable for detecting distal occlusions, clarifying stroke mimics and refining prognosis.
levels.expert:
In a stroke code, the imaging sequence is noncontrast CT, then CTA from arch to vertex, often with CTP, all in one trip. Speed rules: every minute of delay costs neurons.

How I use each piece:
- Noncontrast CT: exclude hemorrhage, gauge ASPECTS, spot a hyperdense vessel. Thrombolysis decisions can proceed from this alone.
- CTA: is there a target for thrombectomy? Read the source images, not just MIPs: proximal occlusions are obvious, but M2 and distal branch occlusions, basilar tip clots and a tandem cervical ICA lesion are easy to miss. Check the arch and access route; a tortuous arch or occluded cervical ICA changes the plan for the interventionalist.
- Collaterals: good leptomeningeal filling beyond the occlusion predicts smaller final infarcts and better outcomes.
- CTP: helps in late or unknown-onset presentations, distal or posterior circulation occlusions and suspected mimics. Check the arterial input and venous output curves before believing any map; motion, bad bolus timing and poor cardiac output produce artifacts.

Pitfalls:
- Chronic carotid occlusion or severe stenosis makes Tmax look alarming without an acute event.
- Seizures can cause hyperperfusion; migraine aura can cause hypoperfusion not in a vascular territory.
- Very early scans can overestimate core; don't exclude a patient on a single number when the clinical picture is compelling.
- Contrast allergy history should not delay a stroke CTA; premedication protocols and reaction management exist, and severe reactions are rare.

CTA also anchors other neurosurgical work: aneurysm planning after SAH, spot sign in ICH, vascular injury screening in penetrating trauma or high-risk cervical fractures, and venous imaging when a young patient has an atypical hemorrhage or headache with papilledema.

keyPoints: CTA images arteries with timed iodinated contrast; finds large vessel occlusion, aneurysms, dissection, spot sign.
Multiphase CTA grades collaterals, a strong predictor of outcome.
CTP maps CBF, CBV, MTT and Tmax; core ≈ rCBF below 30%, at-risk tissue ≈ Tmax above 6 s.
Core + penumbra mismatch supports late-window thrombectomy (DAWN up to 24 h, DEFUSE 3 6–16 h).
Don't delay stroke CTA for kidney function results.
Empty delta sign on contrast CT suggests superior sagittal sinus thrombosis.
